The turnover tax played a significant role in the Soviet economy by influencing consumer
demand and overall economic activity. This tax, levied on the gross revenue of businesses,
was designed to increase the demand for goods by encouraging production and consumption.
By imposing this tax, the government aimed to stimulate economic activity, as businesses
would be incentivized to produce more goods to meet consumer needs, thus generating higher
sales volumes despite the tax burden. However, the effectiveness of the turnover tax often
varied, as it could also lead to increased prices, potentially dampening consumer demand.
Ultimately, while the turnover tax was intended to boost economic activity, its impact was
complex and could result in unintended consequences within the centrally planned economy.

A perfectly competitive firm decides to shut down operations when the market price falls
below its average variable cost (AVC) in the short run. In this situation, the firm is
unable to cover its variable costs, leading to greater losses than if it were to cease
production altogether. Additionally, if the price is less than the minimum average total
cost (ATC), the firm will not be able to sustain its operations in the long run, as it
will not earn sufficient revenue to cover its total costs. Thus, the relationship between
price and average total cost is crucial; when price exceeds maximum average total cost,
the firm can operate profitably, but if it cannot, the firm should consider shutting down
to minimize losses.
answers.explanation: correct because it accurately identifies that a perfectly competitive firm will shut down in the short run when the market price is below the average variable cost, as this indicates that the firm cannot cover its variable costs, while in the long run, if the price is below the minimum average total cost, the firm cannot sustain operations due to insufficient revenue to cover all costs.
